steps.title: Safe science workshop
steps.prompt: Listen to all three safety rules before exploring.
steps.explanation: The rules keep you safe. Keep away from sockets, keep your hands dry, and let grown-ups plug things in.
steps.safety: Electricity is very useful, but it is dangerous. We never put our fingers, or anything else, into a socket. Only grown‑ups plug things in. We never touch electrical things with wet hands.

senseDescriptions.keep_away_from_sockets: We never put our fingers, or anything else, into a socket.
senseDescriptions.keep_hands_dry: We never touch electrical things with wet hands.

steps.title: Power the room
steps.hint: Ask which things must be plugged in to work.
steps.explanation: The television, vacuum cleaner, lamp and dishwasher need electricity to work. The book and chair do not. This lantern uses a flame instead.

source.answerKeyText: Need electricity: television, vacuum cleaner, lamp, dishwasher. Do not: book, lantern (it uses a flame), chair.

steps.shortExplanation: The television, vacuum cleaner, lamp and dishwasher need electricity to work.

steps.title: Then and now
steps.prompt: Find the old tool for each electric helper.
steps.hint: Think about which helper gives light and which one sweeps up dirt.
steps.explanation: A lantern gives light like a lamp. A broom cleans like a vacuum cleaner.

source.answerKeyText: a) a lantern or a candle b) a broom

steps.shortExplanation: Lanterns give light like lamps; brooms clean like vacuum cleaners.

steps.title: Magnet hunt
steps.prompt: Predict for each material, then move the magnet to test it.
steps.explanation: A magnet attracts iron and steel, not all metals. It does not attract aluminium, gold or plastic.
steps.shortExplanation: A magnet attracts iron and steel, not all metals.

steps.title: Magnet discoveries

options.label: A magnet attracts iron and steel
A magnet does not attract all metals

steps.hint: Compare each claim with what happened during the magnet hunt.
steps.explanation: A magnet pulls iron and steel. It does not pull every metal, so the claim about all metals is wrong.

source.answerKeyText: a) NO b) YES c) YES

steps.shortExplanation: A magnet pulls iron and steel.

steps.title: Magnet collection
steps.prompt: Collect only the objects the magnet pulls.
steps.hint: Think about the material of each object, not just its shape.
steps.explanation: The magnet pulls the steel key, iron nail and steel coat hanger. Iron and steel are metals a magnet can pull.

source.answerKeyText: The magnet pulls: steel key, iron nail, steel coat hanger. It does not pull the plastic button, the sock, the leaf or the aluminium foil.

steps.shortExplanation: The magnet pulls the steel key, iron nail and steel coat hanger.

steps.title: Inside the torch
steps.prompt: What powers this torch without a wall socket?
steps.hint: Think about how a torch works when you carry it away from a socket.
steps.explanation: A battery gives the torch electricity to make light. You can carry the torch away from a wall socket.
steps.shortExplanation: A battery gives the torch electricity to make light.

steps.title: Safety promise
steps.hint: Remember the rules about sockets, dry hands and who may plug things in.
steps.explanation: Keep fingers and objects out of sockets. Let grown-ups plug things in, and keep your hands dry near electrical things.

source.answerKeyText: Never put fingers or objects into a socket; only a grown‑up plugs things in; never touch electrical things with wet hands.

steps.safety: Electricity is very useful, but it is dangerous. We never put our fingers, or anything else, into a socket. Only grown‑ups plug things in. We never touch electrical things with wet hands.
steps.shortExplanation: Keep fingers and objects out of sockets; grown-ups handle plugs; keep hands dry near electrical things.

steps.title: Plug, battery or neither?
steps.prompt: Sort the helpers by their power.
steps.hint: Look for a wire and plug, a battery, or an object used by hand.
steps.explanation: The fridge and air conditioner use a plug. The wall clock and torch use batteries. The bicycle and book need neither.

source.answerKeyText: Plug: fridge, air conditioner. Battery: wall clock, torch. Neither: bicycle, book.

steps.shortExplanation: Plugs: fridge, air conditioner; batteries: clock, torch; neither: bicycle, book.

steps.title: Hidden magnets
steps.prompt: Find two places magnets can be used.
steps.hint: Think about objects that need to hold a door or a bag closed.
steps.explanation: Magnets can hold a fridge door seal and a cupboard door catch closed. They help the doors stay shut.

source.answerKeyText: Any two: fridge magnets, the seal on the fridge door, a cupboard door catch, a handbag clasp, a magnetic screwdriver, headphones.

steps.shortExplanation: Magnets can hold a fridge door seal and a cupboard door catch closed.

steps.title: Discovery badges
steps.prompt: Match each discovery to its answer.
steps.hint: Use the safety rules, torch and magnet experiment to help.
steps.explanation: A magnet pulls the steel key. Iron and steel are magnetic metals. A lantern gives light, and a battery powers a torch. Fingers must stay out of sockets.
steps.shortExplanation: Magnets pull steel; lanterns light; batteries power torches; iron and steel are magnetic; avoid sockets.

stickers.meaning: The power that makes lamps, fridges and televisions work.
A machine in the home that runs on electricity.
A small store of electricity you can carry, used in torches and clocks.
A piece of metal that pulls iron and steel towards it.
To pull something towards you without touching it.
A material a magnet will pull, like iron or steel.

homeActivities.text:
The magnet hunt — and the big surprise
Take a fridge magnet around the house. Test a key, a spoon, a coin, an iron nail, a plastic button, a leaf, a piece of aluminium foil, a gold or
silver ring. He predicts each one first.
Here is the surprise: aluminium foil is metal, and gold is metal — but the magnet completely ignores them. So "it is metal" is not the right
answer. The right answer is: a magnet only pulls iron and steel. Let him discover this himself; do not tell him first.
+ −
a battery never touch a socket iron and steel only
torch, toy car, clock
Three things to remember from this unit: batteries, socket safety, and what magnets really pull.
homeActivities.safety:
An adult stays with the child for every activity. No glass, no sockets, no flames, and nothing small enough to swallow is left with a child
alone. Water activities are done in a bowl or the sink, never near electrical items.
